question: The narrator's description of a weighed figure as "a guess dressed up as a fact" (paragraph 7) presents:

options.A: a view the narrator held at the time and later came to revise.
options.B: the narrator's final judgment of the weighing method as a whole.
options.C: Bram's own opinion of the figures that the bank asked him for.
options.D: a belief that Lise shared but chose not to say aloud that night.

question: According to the passage, during the month when Ruud's screen showed estimates shorter than the real waits, written complaints:

options.A: fell by more than a third compared with the winter without a screen.
options.B: dropped at first and then slowly returned to the first winter's level.
options.C: stayed at about the same low level as in the rest of the second winter.
options.D: rose above the level of the first winter, when there was no screen.

question: The passage is best described as an essay in which the author:

options.A: describes how a teacher's methods shaped the paintings the author later exhibited.
options.B: argues that a sketchbook keeps its value only while it is allowed to hold failed work.
options.C: explains why many painters' sketchbooks were taken apart after their owners died.
options.D: argues that museums should stop displaying the sketchbooks of artists in glass cases.

question: The author of Passage B argues that a tree that shed in order to stay clean "would have no reason to follow that schedule." This argument assumes that:

options.A: old trees of a species shed more heavily than young trees of the same species.
options.B: fast-growing trees carry fewer lichens and mosses than slow-growing trees do.
options.C: passengers do not build up on a trunk faster when the trunk is widening faster.
options.D: new outer bark can form only after the old outer bark has completely fallen.
